title: How Much Should an Old Control Group Count? — Pocock Historical Controls, Ibrahim & Chen Power Priors, FDA Trial Exchangeability & Dynamic Borrowing in Richeldi’s Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis FVC Trial

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: In rare diseases like idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, every patient randomized to placebo is precious—yet borrowing an old trial's control group at 100% face value risks bias if care has drifted. Power priors and dynamic borrowing discount historical controls smoothly when old and new data disagree.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Smart Bayesian borrowing speeds rare-disease and pediatric trials while protecting regulators and patients against 'prior-data conflict' when standard of care changes.
keyTakeaways: Pocock (1976) warned that historical controls often differ subtly in baseline severity, imaging, or supportive care.
Ibrahim and Chen's power prior raises the historical likelihood to a fractional exponent a_0 between 0 (ignore history) and 1 (pool fully), scaling effective historical sample size.
Meta-analytic predictive (MAP) priors and Richeldi's IPF lung-function analyses show how dynamic borrowing sheds historical weight automatically if current placebo patients diverge.

vocab.meaning: Weighting the historical dataset's likelihood by exponent a_0 in [0, 1] to control how many 'effective patients' are borrowed.
Divergence between historical control outcomes and concurrent randomized placebo outcomes due to drift in patient mix or care.
The assumption that historical and current control parameters are draws from a shared underlying distribution.

quiz.question: If a historical control group had N_0 = 200 patients and an Ibrahim–Chen fixed power prior uses weight a_0 = 0.25, roughly how many effective historical patients are borrowed?
quiz.explanation: For conjugate exponential-family likelihoods, raising the likelihood to a_0 = 0.25 scales the historical precision/effective sample size to a_0 * N_0 = 50.
